title: Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity: Sparsity: and At

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract states the study compares '40 variants of 30B MoE models and 3.4B dense models trained on a 1 trillion token dataset.' However, Section 3.1 explicitly states 'We conduct experiments on both MoE models (15B total parameters with 2.54B activated, 15A2B) and dense models (1.7B total parameters)' and describes training on varying budgets (400B, 1T, 3T, 3.5T tokens across different tables), not a uniform 1T-token dataset. The model sizes (30B vs 15B, 3.4B vs 1.7B) and token counts directly contradict the body of the paper.

The Introduction claims 'applying key layer gating (G3) yields superior performance improvements compared to SDPA or value gating, reducing PPL by up to 0.3 and improving MMLU significantly' and that 'gating at G3 also leads to better training stability and scaling behavior.' This directly contradicts Section 3.2.1 and Table 1, which report that SDPA output gating (G1, PPL 5.761) and value gating (G2, PPL 5.820) are the most effective, while key gating (G3, row 7) achieves PPL 6.016 (almost identical to baseline 6.026) and only a negligible MMLU gain (59.18 vs 58.79 baseline), far smaller than SDPA's gain (60.82). The paper's own 'Practical Recommendation' also recommends G1, not G3.

The first mini-table ('% PPL ∆': baseline 6.05, SDPA 5.95, value 5.85, key 5.75, query 6.00, dense 6.05) shows 'key' as having the best (lowest) PPL, while the adjacent mini-table ('Position/Value': SDPA -0.26%, value -0.26%, key +0.38%, query +0.39%, dense +0.62%) shows 'key' performing worse than baseline. These two tables in the same figure directly contradict each other regarding whether key gating improves or worsens performance, and both contradict Table 1's result that key gating (G3) barely improves over baseline (6.016 vs 6.026).

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 1 reports for 'v Elementwise G_2': PPL 5.820, HellaSwag 74.38, MMLU 59.17, GSM8k 53.97, C-Eval 61.00. Table 4 reports for the same configuration ('Value Elementwise Gate'): PPL 5.820, HellaSwag 74.38, MMLU 59.17, but GSM8k 51.33 — a different value for an ostensibly identical experiment, an internal inconsistency.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 5.1, Related Works (Gating in Neural Networks)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text cites references [80], [81], and [82] ('state-space models [3, 10, 57, 80]', 'recently proposed DeltaGate model [81]', 'the unseen GatorNet [82] architecture'), but the reference list provided only contains entries up to [71]. These citations point to non-existent or fabricated references, and 'GatorNet' is not a recognized architecture matching any listed citation.

Figure 1's caption describes the right panel as 'Training loss comparison ... over 3T tokens between baseline and SDPA-gated 1.7B dense models,' but Section 3.2.2 refers to the same figure/result set as being under 'the 3.5T token setting' ('Under the 3.5T token setting, gating improves training stability, largely reducing the loss spike (Fig. 1, right)'). The token count for the same experiment/figure is inconsistent (3T vs 3.5T).

The text states 'both baselines and gating variants frequently encounter convergence issues (row 6, 12), with some gating models diverging silently.' However, Table 2 shows only row 12 (a Baseline, not a gating variant) marked as diverged ('-'); no SDPA/gating row exhibits a '-' or any sign of divergence, undermining the claim that gating models diverged.

The abstract claims the gating mechanism provides only 'moderate improvements in long-context extrapolation performance,' but Table 5 shows dramatic gains after YaRN extension: at 64k, baseline 37.51 vs. SDPA-Gate 66.60 (+29 points); at 128k, baseline 31.65 vs. SDPA-Gate 58.82 (+27 points), nearly double the baseline score. This magnitude is inconsistent with the term 'moderate.'

Head-Shared gating is defined as using a reduced score shape 'n × d_k' instead of 'n × q × d_k' (G1) or 'n × k × d_k' (G2), implying a smaller weight matrix (W_θ shared across heads) and thus fewer added parameters. Yet Table 1 lists identical 'Added Param' values for head-shared rows (201 for G1 row 12, 25 for G2 row 13) as their head-specific counterparts (rows 5 and 6), which is mathematically inconsistent with the claimed reduction in score dimensionality (parameter count should scale down roughly by the number of heads, e.g., ~201/32≈6.3M, not 201M).

The diagram depicts the dataflow as G5→Dense→W_O→Concat→SDPA→{G4,G3,G1}→{W_q,W_k,W_v}, which reverses the actual attention computation order (Q/K/V projections occur before SDPA, not after). It also mislabels G1 as connecting to W_v (Value Layer) and omits G2 entirely, whereas the text clearly defines G1 as gating after SDPA output and G2 as gating after the value projection. This contradicts the architecture described in Sections 2.1–2.2 and Figure 1's own caption/text.
